q: Concord, Catawba and Niagara descend from which grape species?
exp: Labrusca is native to North America and gives the pungent aroma usually called foxy. Most of the crop goes to juice, jelly and sweet wine rather than to dry table wine.

q: Vidal Blanc and Seyval Blanc turn up wherever winters are brutal. What are they?
exp: Hybrids cross vinifera with American species to buy the cold hardiness and disease resistance that vinifera lacks. Vidal Blanc's thick skin and high acidity also make it the workhorse grape of North American icewine.

q: Vinifera was thought unplantable in the Finger Lakes until a researcher proved otherwise in the middle of the twentieth century. What was his insight?
opts: Grafting vinifera onto a cold-hardy rootstock
Picking everything before the end of August
Planting only on flat ground below the lakes
Abandoning vinifera in favour of hybrids
exp: Konstantin Frank had worked with vines in a far colder climate and knew the rootstock was the limiting factor: the right one let vinifera come through the winter alive. New York's vinifera industry descends directly from that argument.

q: Humid summers and Viognier make an unlikely pair, yet one East Coast state has built its modern reputation on that grape and on Cabernet Franc. Which state?
exp: Virginia's problem is humidity and its consequent disease pressure rather than cold. Thomas Jefferson tried and failed to grow vinifera at Monticello two centuries before it worked.

q: Norton, a red variety descended from a native American species, is the signature grape of which state?
exp: Norton shrugs off humidity and cold that would destroy vinifera. German settlers built a substantial Missouri wine industry on it long before Prohibition closed it down.

q: Most of the Texas grape crop is grown on a high, flat plateau up near Lubbock. Which appellation is that?
exp: Elevation of around three thousand feet buys the cold nights the rest of the state lacks. Hill Country has more wineries and more visitors, but the High Plains grows the fruit.

q: Two narrow peninsulas reaching out into a Great Lake are the heart of one state's fine-wine production. Which state?
exp: Old Mission and Leelanau are almost surrounded by water, which delays budbreak in spring and holds off frost in autumn, and Riesling and other cool-climate whites do best there. Most of Michigan's acreage is actually Concord and Niagara juice grapes away to the south-west.

q: Hot interior air rises and pulls cold marine air in over a chilly ocean current. Which everyday feature of California vineyards does that produce?
opts: Summer fog that cools the coastal valleys
Deep frost on the valley floor in July
exp: The California Current chills the air sitting above it, and wherever the coastal hills have a gap that air runs inland. It is the reason cool-climate grapes succeed at so warm a latitude.

q: Nights in many western American vineyards fall away sharply after very hot days. Why does that matter in the glass?
opts: Cool nights raise tannin in white grapes only
Cool nights stop the vine from budding
Cool nights hold the acidity in place
Cool nights ferment the fruit on the vine
exp: The hot days build sugar and colour while the cool nights keep the acidity, so a wide diurnal swing lets a grower reach full ripeness without the wine going flat and flabby. Elevation and marine air are the two usual sources of it.

q: Eastern Washington lies a little further north than Bordeaux does. What does that latitude give the vineyards?
opts: A longer growing season than Bordeaux enjoys
exp: The extra daylight helps drive ripeness through a short, intense season. The cold desert nights that follow those long days are what keep the acidity.

q: Why is drip irrigation routine across the American West but tightly restricted in many European appellations?
opts: Much of the West cannot grow vines without water, and no appellation rule bars it
Federal law in the United States requires vineyards to be irrigated
European growers dry-farm purely by preference
American vine varieties need more water than European ones
exp: Rainfall in eastern Washington or the Central Valley simply will not carry a crop. European appellation law has traditionally treated irrigation as a way of inflating yields.

q: National Prohibition ran from 1920 to 1933. Which allowance kept a good many vineyards in the ground?
opts: Sacramental wine and limited home winemaking
Nothing; every commercial vineyard was uprooted
Medicinal alcohol sold through pharmacies alone
Licences to export wine to Canada
exp: Churches could still buy sacramental wine and households could make a set quantity at home, so shipping grapes east became the business. Thick-skinned varieties survived the rail journey best, which is why finer grapes were often pulled out for them.

q: After Repeal, the sale of alcohol in the United States was reorganised into what structure?
opts: A two-tier system of producer and retailer
A state monopoly in every state
A three-tier system of producer, wholesaler and retailer
exp: Producers generally must sell to wholesalers, who sell on to retailers and restaurants. The rules vary state by state, which is why a wine easy to buy in one state can be unobtainable in the next.

q: Robert Mondavi coined a name for barrel-aged Sauvignon Blanc in the 1960s, and other wineries then borrowed it. What is the term?
exp: Fume Blanc is a federally approved synonym for Sauvignon Blanc, so the 75 percent varietal minimum applies to it, but no law requires the oak the name implies. The renaming rescued a grape that was then selling poorly in California.

q: European vineyards were rescued from phylloxera in the nineteenth century by what American contribution?
opts: American pesticides applied to the soil
exp: Vitis riparia, rupestris and berlandieri tolerate the root louse where vinifera cannot, so vinifera is grafted onto them. The louse had reached Europe on American vines in the first place, which is the irony of the fix.

q: Which species accounts for nearly all of the world's quality wine production?
exp: Vitis vinifera is the Eurasian species behind essentially every classic wine grape. The American species appear mainly as rootstock parents and in hybrid breeding.
